content:
Let \(a_{ij}=1\) if the square in row \(i\), column \(j\) is red, and \(0\) otherwise.

For a fixed \(j\), define  
\[
P_i(j)=a_{ij}+a_{i,j+1}+a_{i,j+2}.
\]
From every \(2\times 3\) rectangle having exactly two red squares,
\[
P_i(j)+P_{i+1}(j)=2,\qquad P_{i+2}(j)=P_i(j).
\]
So for fixed \(j\), \(P_i(j)\) alternates between some \(t_j\) and \(2-t_j\) by row parity.

Similarly, from the \(3\times 2\) condition, for fixed \(i\),
\[
Q_j(i)=a_{ij}+a_{i+1,j}+a_{i+2,j}
\]
alternates between some \(s_i\) and \(2-s_i\) by column parity.

Summing a \(3\times 3\) block in two ways forces these alternating values to be either \(c\) or \(2-c\) according to parity of \(i+j\). Since the cells are binary, \(c\) cannot be \(0\) or \(2\); otherwise a row would need a triple sum \(0\) next to a triple sum \(2\), impossible. Thus \(c=1\).

Hence every row has exactly one red square in any three consecutive columns, and every column has exactly one red square in any three consecutive rows. Therefore the pattern is \(3\)-periodic in both directions, and each \(3\times 3\) block has exactly one red in each row and column, i.e. \(3\) red squares.

A \(9\times 11\) rectangle consists of a \(9\times 9\) part, which has \(9\) such \(3\times 3\) blocks, giving \(9\cdot 3=27\) red squares, plus a \(9\times 2\) strip. In any two columns of a \(3\times 3\) permutation block there are exactly \(2\) red squares, so the strip contributes \(3\cdot 2=6\).

Total:
\[
27+6=33.
\]

\[
\boxed{33}
\]
